data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive, pragmatic decision rule based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness), where 'preference' signals a theory has survived severe tests and thus possesses higher content and potential truth-likeness, without assigning it logical probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be formally defined or calculated without relying on inductive assumptions (as argued by Miller and Tich\u00fd).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for survival implicitly assumes that the future will resemble the past (the problem of induction).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on' a theory logically entails an expectation of success that contradicts the rejection of probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between logical probability (which decreases with content) and corroboration (which increases with severity of tests passed). The rational agent prefers the theory with higher verisimilitude not because it is 'more likely true' in an inductive sense, but because it has withstood attempts to falsify it, making it the best available conjecture for action. This is a methodological rule, not an inductive inference.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
